RAM (Random Access Memory) is temporary storage for your computer to hold data while it's running programs. It lets the CPU access files quickly when they're needed right now—like keeping open documents or game assets ready so you don't have to reload them constantly. When you turn off your PC, RAM clears out and everything stored there disappears (that's why you need a hard drive for permanent storage).

Btrfs (B-tree Filesystem) is a modern Linux file system that was designed with several advanced features like copy-on-write, built-in compression and checksumming for data integrity, snapshot support, and RAID capabilities all in one filesystem. It's been around since 2013 but gained more popularity as it became the default root filesystem on many Fedora releases starting from version 40.

sudo means superuser do – it lets you run a command with the permissions of your system's administrator (root) instead of just yourself. On Fedora, most administrative tasks require sudo because they need access to files or settings that regular users can't touch.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is connection-oriented and reliable - it establishes a connection before sending data, ensures packets arrive in order, and retransmits lost or corrupted packets. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless and faster but less reliable - it sends datagrams without establishing connections first, doesn't guarantee delivery or ordering, and may drop packets if the network gets congested.

TCP uses ports for each application's data stream while UDP typically shares a single port across all applications using that protocol.
